title: THE BIBLE’S SEXUAL SCANDALS WERE NEVER JUST ABOUT “BAD WOMEN”—SO WHY HAVE WE BEEN LETTING THE MEN WALK AWAY?
paragraphs: THE BIBLE’S SEXUAL SCANDALS WERE NEVER JUST ABOUT “BAD WOMEN”—SO WHY HAVE WE BEEN LETTING THE MEN WALK AWAY?

The stories we thought exposed sinful women also expose powerful men, hidden lust, religious hypocrisy, sexual exploitation, and the devastating consequences of unchecked desire. And when Jesus enters the story, nobody gets to hide behind someone else’s shame.
There is something deeply disturbing about the way some of us have learned to tell the Bible’s most uncomfortable stories.
We remember the woman caught in adultery.
But we rarely ask where the man was.
We remember Bathsheba bathing.
But we sometimes forget David was watching.
We remember Tamar’s pregnancy.
But we forget Judah was the man who propositioned her.
We remember Samson falling because of Delilah.
But we forget that Samson had been making reckless decisions long before Delilah entered the story.
We remember the Samaritan woman’s five husbands.
But we often speak as though Jesus told us why those marriages ended.
He didn't.
And perhaps one of the most dangerous things we can do with Scripture is become so confident in the shame we assign to someone else that we stop hearing what God is exposing in us.
Because the Bible does not tell these stories so men can congratulate themselves for being righteous while women carry the weight of sexual shame.
It tells the truth about human sin.
Even when that truth embarrasses kings.
Even when it exposes patriarchs.
Even when it confronts religious leaders.
Even when it shatters the reputation of men we have admired since childhood.
And if we read carefully, we discover something breathtaking.
God is not afraid to tell the truth about the people He used.
Not because their sins were acceptable.
But because His grace was never dependent upon pretending those sins never happened.
Before you continue, consider one question.
What if the person you have spent years condemning in a Bible story was never the only person God wanted you to examine?
What if you have been looking at the scandal...
while missing the mirror?
There is a Hebrew word that appears in the Bible's account of David and Bathsheba: שָׁלַח (shalach).
It means “to send.”
A simple word.
Until you notice how David uses the power to send people in 2 Samuel 11.
He sends to inquire about Bathsheba.
He sends messengers to bring her.
He sends word to Joab.
He sends Uriah back toward a battlefield where death awaits him.
And suddenly the story becomes more than an account of forbidden desire.
It becomes a terrifying picture of what happens when a man with authority begins treating other human beings as instruments of his own appetite.
David was not an ordinary man looking for love.
He was Israel's king.
He had armies.
He had servants.
He had influence.
He had power.
Bathsheba was identified as the wife of Uriah the Hittite.
David knew she was married.
And still, he sent for her.

The biblical text tells us that David took her and lay with her (2 Samuel 11:4). It does not describe Bathsheba's internal thoughts or establish that she freely consented. The enormous imbalance of power matters, and we must not invent consent where Scripture does not give it.
Yet how many times have people turned this account into a warning about a woman's clothing, beauty, or bathing?
Scripture does not say Bathsheba was attempting to seduce the king.
It says David saw her.
David inquired.
David sent.
David took.
And when the prophet Nathan finally confronted the scandal, he did not approach Bathsheba with an accusation.
He approached David.
“You are the man,” Nathan declared (2 Samuel 12:7, KJV).
Four words.
Enough to tear the disguise off a king.
Imagine the silence.
David had tried to bury the evidence beneath military orders and a carefully arranged death.
Uriah, a faithful soldier, had refused the comforts of home while his fellow soldiers remained in battle.
And David, the king who should have protected him, arranged his destruction.
The man who had written songs about God had committed adultery, abused royal power, and orchestrated a killing.
Nathan did not soften the truth because David was anointed.
He did not excuse the crime because David had once defeated Goliath.
He did not say the king's ministry was too important to be questioned.
He exposed him.
And David finally said, “I have sinned against the LORD” (2 Samuel 12:13, KJV).
That confession mattered.
But it did not bring Uriah back.
It did not erase the harm Bathsheba had experienced.
It did not prevent the consequences that followed.
And this is something we desperately need to recover in the Church.
Forgiveness is real. But forgiveness is not the same thing as pretending the damage never happened.
God's mercy does not make a victim's suffering insignificant.
Repentance is not a public-relations strategy.
A man cannot use the language of grace to escape the responsibility of telling the truth.
And a leader cannot demand silence from the wounded simply because his reputation is at stake.
If Nathan could confront a king, the Church should never become a hiding place for powerful men who refuse accountability.
But David is not the only man Scripture exposes.
Travel backward into Genesis 38.
There you will find Tamar.
A woman whose story has sometimes been reduced to sexual scandal without sufficient attention to the injustice that preceded it.
Tamar was Judah's daughter-in-law.
After the deaths of her first two husbands, Judah promised that she would eventually be given to his younger son, Shelah, according to the family obligations of that time.
But the promise was not fulfilled.
Tamar was left waiting.
Her future was suspended by a man who possessed authority over the family arrangement.
Then Judah encountered a veiled woman whom he believed to be a prostitute.
He approached her and negotiated a sexual encounter.
He did not recognize that she was Tamar.
Later, when Judah learned that Tamar was pregnant, he demanded severe punishment.
“Bring her forth, and let her be burnt” (Genesis 38:24, KJV).
Can you feel the hypocrisy?
The man who participated in the encounter was ready to condemn the woman for the pregnancy that resulted from it.
He wanted judgment.
Until the evidence reached him.
Tamar produced the personal items Judah had given her as a pledge.
And suddenly the man who was prepared to pronounce judgment had to confront his own conduct.
Judah acknowledged, “She hath been more righteous than I” (Genesis 38:26, KJV).
The Hebrew expression is צָדְקָה מִמֶּנִּי (tsadeqah mimmeni).
In context, Judah is acknowledging that Tamar was more in the right than he was, because he had failed to give her his son Shelah as promised.
That does not mean every detail of Tamar's actions becomes a universal moral example.
It means the biblical narrative refuses to allow Judah's hypocrisy to stand.
He was prepared to punish someone while refusing to acknowledge his own responsibility.
And isn't that frighteningly familiar?
A woman becomes pregnant, and everyone wants to know what she did.
A man fathers a child, and people sometimes rush to protect his future.
A woman confesses a sexual mistake, and her reputation can follow her for years.
A man confesses the same kind of wrongdoing, and someone may call him a promising leader who simply stumbled.
These double standards are not the righteousness of God.
They are human favoritism dressed in religious language.
And the story becomes even more astonishing when we turn to Matthew 1:3.
Tamar appears in the genealogy of Jesus Christ.
Read that again.
The woman whose story involved family injustice, deception, and public disgrace is named in the recorded ancestry of the Messiah.
Not because God approved of every action in the story.
But because human brokenness did not prevent God from accomplishing His redemptive purposes.
The genealogy of Jesus does not conceal the complicated history of His human family line.
It tells us that the Savior entered a world already stained by the very sins He came to confront.
Not by calling evil good.
But by bringing redemption into a history where evil had done terrible damage.
Then there is Samson.
How many sermons have reduced his downfall to one message?
Beware of Delilah.
Certainly, Delilah betrayed him.
Judges 16 makes that clear.
But Samson's spiritual collapse did not begin the day Delilah learned the secret of his strength.
Long before that, Samson had repeatedly pursued his desires without the wisdom and self-control his calling required.
Judges 14 records his insistence on marrying a Philistine woman despite his parents' objections.
Judges 16:1 records his visit to a prostitute in Gaza.
Later, his relationship with Delilah becomes the setting of his betrayal and capture.
Delilah was responsible for her deception.
But Samson was responsible for his own choices.
We must stop treating women as though they possess mysterious powers that remove men's responsibility for their decisions.
A man's desire does not become someone else's moral responsibility simply because he finds that person attractive.
James 1:14 teaches that each person is tempted when drawn away by their own desire.
The Greek word ἐπιθυμία (epithymia) refers to desire or longing; in this context, desire that entices toward sin.
Notice where James places responsibility.
Not automatically on the person being desired.
But on the person being drawn away by their own desire.
That truth confronts everyone.
Men and women alike.
We cannot outsource repentance.
We cannot blame another person's appearance for the choices we willingly make.
We cannot build a theology of holiness that requires women to carry responsibility for men's thoughts while men remain unaccountable for their own hearts.
Jesus Himself made this painfully clear.
In Matthew 5:28, He warned against looking at another person with lustful intent.
The Greek expression πρὸς τὸ ἐπιθυμῆσαι αὐτήν (pros to epithymēsai autēn) concerns looking at a woman with the purpose of lusting after her.
Jesus was addressing the moral responsibility of the person doing the looking.
He was not teaching that the person being looked at automatically bears the guilt.
And the solution Jesus demanded was not to blame the woman.
It was to deal radically with the sin in one's own life.
Not through literal self-mutilation, but through the uncompromising rejection of what leads us into sin.
That is a far more uncomfortable sermon.
Because it removes our favorite excuse.
And perhaps that is why we do not always want to preach it.
Then the story takes us into a room filled with religious accusation.
A woman is brought before Jesus.
She has been caught in adultery, according to her accusers.
The scribes and Pharisees place her in the center.
Not gently.
Not privately.
Publicly.
They ask Jesus whether she should be stoned.
And here is the question that has troubled countless careful readers.
Where is the man?
Leviticus 20:10 and Deuteronomy 22:22 address both parties in adultery.
Yet in this scene, only the woman is presented.
The passage does not tell us what happened to the man.
We should not invent an answer.
But his absence from the accusation is conspicuous.
The accusers were not simply seeking justice.
John 8:6 explicitly says they were testing Jesus, seeking grounds to accuse Him.
The woman had become a weapon in someone else's religious confrontation.
And Jesus refused to play their game.
He stooped and wrote on the ground.
We are not told what He wrote.
Theories abound, but Scripture does not identify the words.
Then Jesus spoke.
“He that is without sin among you, let him first cast a stone at her” (John 8:7, KJV).
One sentence.
And the atmosphere changed.
The men who had arrived ready to expose someone else's sin were suddenly confronted with their own.
One by one, they left.
Jesus then said to the woman, “Neither do I condemn thee: go, and sin no more” (John 8:11, KJV).
There is something essential we must preserve here.
Jesus did not declare adultery harmless.
He called her away from sin.
But He also refused to let religious hypocrisy have the final word over her life.
Mercy did not abolish holiness.
Holiness did not extinguish mercy.
They met in Jesus Christ.

An important textual note belongs here: the account of the woman caught in adultery, traditionally placed in John 7:53–8:11, is absent from several of the earliest surviving Greek manuscripts of John's Gospel and appears in different locations in some manuscript traditions. Many modern Bible translations identify this textual issue. Christians who teach this passage should acknowledge that history rather than conceal it. Its familiar portrait of mercy and repentance is consistent with themes clearly established elsewhere in the New Testament, but its textual status should be handled carefully.
And even with that qualification, the questions raised by this traditional account are worth examining alongside the rest of Scripture.
Why are we sometimes more eager to expose a sinner than to restore a human being?
Why can public shame feel more satisfying than private repentance?
Why do we sometimes enjoy the downfall of someone whose struggles resemble our own?
The Gospel does not invite us to become spectators at someone else's humiliation.
It calls us to face our own need for mercy.
And now consider the woman at the well.
John 4.
Jesus meets a Samaritan woman and asks her for water.
Their conversation moves from ordinary thirst to living water.
Then Jesus tells her to call her husband.
She answers that she has no husband.
Jesus responds that she has had five husbands and that the man she currently has is not her husband.
For generations, this woman has frequently been described as sexually promiscuous.
But the text does not explain how those five marriages ended.
She may have experienced divorce, widowhood, abandonment, or circumstances the narrative simply does not reveal.
We are not told.
And when Scripture does not tell us something, humility requires that we stop pretending it does.
Jesus identifies the truth about her situation.
But He does not give us permission to invent a detailed history of her sexual conduct.
What He does reveal is something much greater.
He speaks to her about worship.
He reveals Himself as Messiah.
And she becomes a witness to her community.
The woman who came to draw water leaves her water jar and goes to tell others about Jesus.
The encounter moves from exposure to revelation.
From personal history to living water.
From being known by Jesus to inviting others to know Him.
And that should make every one of us examine the way we speak about people whose histories we do not fully understand.
Someone may have been divorced several times.
You do not know every betrayal they survived.
Someone may be raising a child alone.
You do not know the circumstances that brought them there.
Someone may carry a sexual history they deeply regret.
You do not know how much manipulation, coercion, loneliness, fear, or personal failure is involved.
This does not mean sin is imaginary.
It means human stories are often more complicated than the labels we assign.
Jesus knew the truth about the Samaritan woman without reducing her to a caricature.
We should learn from Him.
But perhaps the most devastating evidence that Scripture exposes men's sexual wrongdoing comes from stories we would sometimes rather skip entirely.
Genesis 34 tells of Dinah and Shechem.
The narrative describes Shechem taking Dinah and violating her.
Whatever complexities appear in the subsequent negotiations, the original violation is not something to romanticize.
Then there is 2 Samuel 13.
Amnon desires his half-sister Tamar.
He manipulates circumstances to isolate her.
She pleads with him.
She resists.
He refuses to listen.
And he rapes her.
Afterward, the text describes his hatred toward her.
The same man who claimed to desire her now wants her removed from his presence.
Tamar is left devastated.
The biblical narrative does not portray her as the seductress.
It shows the terrible destruction caused by Amnon's violence and the failure of those around her to provide justice.
And there is an especially painful detail.
Tamar asks, “Whither shall I cause my shame to go?” (2 Samuel 13:13, KJV).
She is speaking from within a culture in which the consequences of sexual violence could devastate a woman's social standing.
But the fact that Tamar experiences shame does not mean she is morally guilty for what Amnon did.
The shame imposed upon a victim is not proof of the victim's sin.
Someone needs to hear that.
Perhaps someone reading this has spent years carrying guilt for an act of violence committed against them.
Perhaps someone has been told to remain silent because the person who harmed them was respected.
Perhaps someone has been pressured to forgive before anyone was willing to acknowledge what happened.
Listen carefully.
What another person did to violate you is not your moral failure.
God does not require you to rename abuse as love.
He does not require you to call exploitation a misunderstanding.
He does not require you to surrender your safety to prove that you have forgiven.
Forgiveness and reconciliation are not identical.
Forgiveness does not remove the need for truth, protection, accountability, or lawful justice.
And the Church must never use spiritual language to shield those who harm the vulnerable.
Jesus warned severely against causing the vulnerable to stumble (Matthew 18:6).
The God of Scripture is not indifferent to the suffering of those who have been violated.
Psalm 34:18 tells us, “The LORD is nigh unto them that are of a broken heart” (KJV).
Not every wound heals quickly.
Not every story receives earthly justice.
Not every survivor is ready to speak publicly.
And no one should be forced to turn their trauma into a testimony for the comfort of an audience.
But the wounded are not invisible to God.
He sees.
He knows.
And His justice is not canceled by another person's status, title, or religious reputation.
Now we must turn the mirror toward ourselves.
Because it would be easy to read all of this and simply conclude that men are the problem.
That would miss the Gospel too.
Scripture does not teach that women are morally innocent and men are morally corrupt.
Women also make sinful choices.
Men also experience exploitation and violence.
Both men and women are accountable before God.
Both are capable of deception, lust, pride, selfishness, and cruelty.
Both can be wounded.
Both need grace.
Romans 3:23 does not divide humanity into one guilty sex and one innocent sex.
“For all have sinned, and come short of the glory of God” (KJV).
All.
The problem is not that Scripture refuses to confront women's sin.
The problem is that readers sometimes confront women's sin selectively while minimizing the sins of men, especially when those men possess authority.
And selective righteousness is not righteousness.
It is partiality.
The Gospel leaves no room for the man who thinks his private pornography habit is less serious than a woman's public sexual history simply because no one knows about it.
It leaves no room for the husband who demands fidelity while maintaining secret affairs.
It leaves no room for the pastor who preaches purity while exploiting someone under his spiritual care.
It leaves no room for the woman who uses manipulation, deceit, or sexual betrayal and then refuses responsibility.
It leaves no room for the person who delights in exposing someone else's past while carefully concealing their own.
The cross confronts all of us.
And here is where the story becomes personal.
Maybe you have never been a king like David.
But you know what it feels like to hide something.
Maybe you have never stood where Judah stood.
But you remember a time when you judged someone for a sin you secretly excused in yourself.
Maybe you have never lived Samson's life.
But you recognize the slow erosion of conviction when desire repeatedly wins the argument.
Maybe you have never stood among the accusers in John 8.
But you have held someone else's failure in your mind like a stone.
Maybe you have been the one publicly judged.
Maybe you have been the one privately wounded.
Maybe you have been both the sinner and the person sinned against in different chapters of your life.
And somewhere beneath all the defenses, there is a question you cannot quite escape.
What does Jesus do with someone who knows the truth about their own life and cannot rewrite the past?
This is where the Gospel becomes more than a moral lecture.
Because Christianity does not announce that good people have finally found a way to separate themselves from bad people.
It announces that Jesus Christ came to save sinners.
The apostle Paul wrote in 1 Timothy 1:15:
“Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners; of whom I am chief” (KJV).
Paul did not say that Christ came to save people who could successfully manage their reputations.
He came for sinners.
People whose guilt is real.
People whose excuses have run out.
People whose histories contain things they cannot undo.
But we must understand grace correctly.
Grace is not permission to continue abusing others.
Grace is not a spiritual escape hatch for powerful offenders.
Grace is not a demand that wounded people immediately trust the people who hurt them.
Grace is God's undeserved favor, revealed supremely in Jesus Christ, that forgives and transforms those who turn to Him in faith.
The Greek word χάρις (charis) is commonly translated “grace.”
In the New Testament, it can refer to favor, gift, or gracious generosity, depending on context.
And Ephesians 2:8–9 declares that salvation is by grace through faith, not the achievement of human works.
But the passage does not stop there.
Ephesians 2:10 teaches that we are created in Christ Jesus for good works.
Grace saves us.
And grace begins changing the way we live.
That is why genuine repentance matters.

The Greek noun μετάνοια (metanoia) means repentance, involving a change of mind or orientation; in the biblical call to repentance, it is not merely feeling sorry but turning toward God in a way that bears fruit.
The person who has sinned cannot purchase innocence with a dramatic apology.
The person who has harmed someone cannot demand that the wounded person immediately restore the relationship.
The person who has hidden behind religious respectability cannot substitute ministry activity for integrity.
Real repentance tells the truth.
Real repentance stops defending what God condemns.
Real repentance accepts responsibility.
Real repentance seeks to repair harm where possible, without treating restitution as a purchase of forgiveness.
And real repentance begins with surrender to Jesus Christ.
Not because we can repair ourselves perfectly.
But because the One who died for our sins and rose again is able to make us new.
Consider the woman Luke describes in Luke 7:36–50.
She enters a Pharisee's house while Jesus is reclining at a meal.
Luke identifies her as a woman known in the city as a sinner, but does not specify that her sin was sexual.
That detail matters.
We should not add sexual accusations to a person's story simply because the text uses the word “sinner.”
She weeps at Jesus' feet.
Her tears fall.
She wipes His feet with her hair.
She kisses them and anoints them.
Simon the Pharisee watches.
And in his heart, he judges.
If Jesus were truly a prophet, Simon thinks, He would know what kind of woman this is.
But Jesus does know.
He knows the woman.
And He knows Simon.
That is the part we sometimes forget.
The Lord who sees the tears of the publicly disgraced also sees the pride of the privately respectable.
Jesus tells a parable about two debtors who are forgiven.
Then He turns toward the woman while speaking to Simon.
“Seest thou this woman?” (Luke 7:44, KJV).
What a question.
Simon had seen her.
But only through the lens of her reputation.
He saw a category.
A scandal.
A reason to feel superior.
Jesus saw a person.
And then Jesus declared to her, “Thy sins are forgiven” (Luke 7:48, KJV).
The story does not deny that she was a sinner.
It reveals that her sin was not beyond the reach of divine mercy.
Her faith was directed toward the One who could forgive.
And perhaps that is the invitation this entire article has been moving toward.
Not merely to change how we discuss women in the Bible.
Not merely to confront male hypocrisy.
Not merely to expose religious double standards.
But to recognize that every human being must ultimately stand before Jesus Christ without a disguise.
The abused person does not need to accept blame for the abuse.
The guilty person does need to acknowledge guilt.
The self-righteous person needs to repent of pride.
The broken person needs the hope of God's mercy.
And every one of us needs the Savior.
Because the Gospel is not the story of Jesus choosing a morally superior group of people.
It is the story of the sinless Son of God giving Himself for sinners.
At the cross, we see how seriously God takes evil.
Sin is not dismissed as harmless.
And we see how astonishingly far divine love goes to redeem.
Christ bore our sins.
He died.
He was buried.
And He rose again, as proclaimed in 1 Corinthians 15:3–4.
The resurrection is not a sentimental ending added to a tragic story.
It is the announcement that sin and death do not have the final word over those who belong to Christ.
And that changes everything.
David's sin was not made righteous.
Judah's hypocrisy was not made admirable.
Samson's recklessness was not made wise.
Amnon's violence was not made excusable.
The religious accusers' cruelty was not made holy.
But none of these stories can overturn the central truth of the Gospel.
God is holy.
Humanity is fallen.
Jesus Christ is the Savior.
And His grace calls us into truth, repentance, forgiveness, and transformation.
Maybe you are reading this with tears in your eyes because someone once used the Bible to shame you for what another person did.
Maybe you have quietly believed that your sexual history disqualifies you from ever being loved by God.
Maybe you are a man who has excused lust, deception, or betrayal for years while judging women more harshly than yourself.
Maybe you are a woman who has hidden destructive choices behind the assumption that only men should be confronted.
Maybe you are a Christian leader who needs to stop protecting an image and start telling the truth.
Or maybe you are simply exhausted from pretending to be cleaner, stronger, and more spiritually stable than you really are.
Hear this.
You do not have to manufacture an innocent past to come to Jesus.
You do have to come honestly.
You cannot rewrite yesterday.
But through Christ, yesterday does not have to be the master of tomorrow.
And that is why our message at Gospel Warrior is not built around the fantasy that Christians never fall.
It is built around the truth that Jesus Christ saves, restores, disciplines, and transforms people who turn to Him.
Not by denying the scandal.
Not by hiding the victims.
Not by protecting the guilty from consequences.
Not by reducing grace to a slogan.
But by bringing sinners into the light of truth and offering redemption through the crucified and risen Christ.
If this article has exposed something you need to surrender, do not rush past that conviction.
Sit with it.
Open the Scriptures.
Pray honestly.
If you have sinned against someone, stop justifying it. Seek godly accountability, make appropriate restitution, and respect the other person's boundaries.

If you have been harmed, remember that another person's sin does not define your worth. Seek safety, wise support, and appropriate professional or pastoral care from people who will protect rather than silence you.

And if you have been living beneath the crushing weight of shame, remember that Jesus calls people out of darkness not to entertain an audience with their humiliation, but to bring them into His light.
There may be someone in your family who needs to read this.
A son who has been taught that masculine desire is uncontrollable.
A daughter who has been made to feel responsible for someone else's choices.
A husband who needs to confront his double standards.
A wife who needs to hear that God sees her suffering.
A church leader who needs to remember that authority increases responsibility.
A young believer who has confused purity with public reputation.
Or someone who has abandoned church because religious people seemed more interested in scandal than restoration.
Not merely because it may reach more people, but because biblical truth deserves to be discussed beyond the safety of familiar circles.
And I want to ask you something personal.
When you look at these biblical accounts, which truth confronts you most deeply?
That men must be held accountable for their own choices?
That victims should never be blamed for the harm committed against them?
That religious hypocrisy can hide beneath the appearance of holiness?
Or that Jesus still offers forgiveness to repentant sinners whose past cannot be undone?
You can simply write, “Jesus, search my heart.”
Or “No more hiding.”
Or “Christ is still healing me.”
You do not have to reveal private trauma, name anyone, or disclose details you are not ready to share.
Sometimes a few honest words are enough to begin a meaningful conversation.
And sometimes someone else reading the comments discovers that they are not the only person trying to find their way back to God.
We want this community to be a place where Scripture is taken seriously, Jesus Christ remains central, and difficult truths are approached with both courage and compassion.
And if you have been receiving encouragement, conviction, or spiritual nourishment through Gospel Warrior, I want to invite you to consider something deeper.
Our mission is not simply to publish articles that people read for a few minutes and forget.
We want to help people keep opening their Bibles after the emotional moment has passed.
We want struggling believers to find biblical encouragement.
We want seekers to encounter the message of Jesus.
We want families to have resources that help them grow in faith.
We want discipleship to continue beyond a single post.
Those resources are part of our desire to make biblical learning and spiritual nourishment more accessible.
But continuing and expanding this work also requires practical support.
Writing, preparing resources, maintaining a growing library, and reaching more people all involve time, effort, and expense.
But I want to be biblically careful here.

Scripture teaches us to give willingly, not under pressure or compulsion (2 Corinthians 9:7). Supporting your local church, caring for your household, and helping those in need remain important responsibilities.
These items are not substitutes for Scripture or spiritual growth, and the discount is not the reason to pursue Christ.
They are simply one way we can express gratitude to those who help sustain the ministry.
Perhaps someone who has silently carried shame for years will read it.
Perhaps someone who has used spiritual authority irresponsibly will finally begin to confront their conduct.
Perhaps a believer who has been drifting will return to the Scriptures.
Perhaps someone who has never understood the Gospel will begin asking who Jesus really is.
We cannot promise what any particular post will accomplish.
But we can faithfully proclaim Christ and trust God with the fruit.
Because ultimately, Gospel Warrior is not the Savior.
A social media page is not the Church.
And no amount of engagement can replace repentance, faith, obedience, and genuine fellowship with other believers.
Jesus Christ is the Savior.
And the mission is worth supporting only insofar as it faithfully points people toward Him.
Before you leave, return with me to the question that began this story.
Where was the man?
It was a question about a woman brought before religious accusers.
But perhaps, after everything we have read, we should ask another question.
Where are we standing?
Beside David, hoping no one discovers what we have done?
Beside Judah, condemning someone for a sin in which we share responsibility?
Beside Samson, blaming another person for choices we refuse to confront?
Beside Simon the Pharisee, examining someone else's reputation while ignoring our own pride?
Or at the feet of Jesus, finally willing to tell the truth?
Because the most important question is not whether you can identify the worst sinner in the room.
It is whether you are willing to come to the only One in the room who has never sinned.
And receive the mercy you could never earn.
The Bible's sexual scandals are not invitations to despise women.
They are not invitations to despise men.
They are warnings about what sin can do to human beings, relationships, families, and communities.
They are reminders that power without integrity becomes dangerous.
That desire without self-control can become destructive.
That religious language without humility can become cruel.
And that grace without truth becomes a counterfeit of the Gospel.
But above all, they lead us toward the Savior who is both full of grace and truth (John 1:14).
So put down the stone you were never qualified to throw.
Confess the sin you have been trying to conceal.
Protect the person whose suffering others have tried to minimize.
Tell the truth, even when the truth is costly.
And come to Jesus.
Not as the hero of your own carefully edited story.
But as a human being who needs the mercy of God.
Because one day, when all the excuses have fallen silent, the question will not be how successfully you exposed another person's darkness.
It will be whether you responded to the Light when He called you out of your own.
The hands that were pierced for sinners are still the reason our darkest chapters do not have to be our final ones.
